zh.technical_title: 面向物理 AI 的记忆建模
zh.technical_text: 我关注过去的经历如何通过记忆影响智能体未来的行为与决策，以及我们如何塑造这种影响。
zh.lifelong_text: 如何让有着不同性格和成败经历的人，尽可能不必依赖过人的毅力与耐力，也能保持面对现实、采取成功者会做出的行动，并逐渐改善生活的能力？
zh.title: 走出成败的循环
paragraphs: 做科研让我反复感受到，努力与结果之间可能隔着很长时间。许多尝试没有得到预期的结果，时间久了，连继续尝试的信心也会受到影响。我开始想：为什么有些人越来越成功，而另一些人却在一次次受挫后，逐渐失去了改变处境的力量？
在人类社会中，“我能做到”的信心往往需要接连的成功来积累，却可能因少数几次重大失败而瓦解。这种积累与瓦解的不对称，会让失败循环更容易形成，让成功循环更难建立和维持。成功带来的资源与机会，还可能进一步拉大这种差距。
我们常把坚持下来的原因归于毅力，但每个人的承受力都有边界。即使曾经坚韧、成功，也可能被后来的挫折击垮。在我看来，把走出困境的希望全寄托于个人毅力或过往成功，忽略人所处的条件和能够获得的支持，过于唯心，也不是充分的科学方法论。
一篇给我启发的论文，是 Zhou 等人发表于 Science 的论文：History of winning remodels thalamo-PFC circuit to reinforce social dominance（2017）。在实验条件下，多次获胜会增强小鼠特定脑回路的连接，使它们在之后的竞争中更容易保持优势。通俗地说，获胜的经历会留在大脑里，影响下一次竞争时的表现。
这篇研究还有一个让我在意的发现：人工激活相关脑区，能让原本处于劣势的小鼠更主动地竞争，甚至战胜原先赢过它的对手。在这个实验里，过去的战绩并没有完全决定之后的表现。我想继续追问：对于人，我们能否也找到某种方法，让人即使经历过失败，也能采取成功者会做出的行动？
纯粹的精神胜利也无法解决这个问题。阿Q可以在想象中把失败解释成胜利，暂时得到安慰，但现实中的处境并没有因此改善。如果这种解释让人回避问题、忽略反馈，它还可能使改变更难发生。自我安慰可以帮助人缓一口气，却不能替代解决问题所需要的判断和行动。
我想用一生寻找一种更本质、更基础的方法：让有着不同性格和成败经历的人，尽可能不必依赖过人的毅力与耐力，也能保持面对现实、采取成功者会做出的行动，并逐渐改善生活的能力。
AI 正在改变工作，也可能动摇许多人赖以获得收入、社会认可和身份感的方式。当一个人长期积累的技能不再被需要时，他该如何理解自己的价值，又如何找到继续行动的方向？这个问题的迫切性远不止于我个人，它关乎越来越多的人，也关乎整个人类如何面对这些变化。
对我而言，这也是攻读 Doctor of Philosophy 的意义之一：认真追问一个重要的问题，不把寻找答案的方式限定在某个学科之内。我希望带着自己在人工智能、记忆与学习方面积累的知识，为它提供一个不同的视角。

zh.figure_caption: 第 0 天（蓝色区域），研究者通过光刺激帮助小鼠获胜。左图：横轴是天数，纵轴是比原来提升的名次；停止刺激后，红色组保持优势，橙色组回到原排名。右图：获胜 2–5 次的小鼠中，4/13 只保持新排名；获胜 6–20 次的 11 只全部保持。n 和柱内数字表示小鼠数量，*** 表示两组差异显著（p < 0.001）。

en.technical_text: I study how past experiences shape an agent’s future behavior and decisions through memory, and how we can shape that influence.
en.lifelong_title: Beyond the cycle of success and failure
en.lifelong_text: How can people with different personalities and histories of success and failure sustain the ability to face reality, take the actions a successful person would take, and improve their lives, without depending on exceptional willpower or endurance?
en.title: Beyond the cycle of success and failure
paragraphs: Research has repeatedly shown me how far effort can be from a clear result. Many attempts do not work out as expected. Over time, even the confidence to try again can suffer. I began to wonder: why do some people become increasingly successful, while others gradually lose the ability to change their circumstances after repeated setbacks?

In human society, the confidence that “I can do this” often takes a succession of successes to build, yet a few major failures may undo it. This asymmetry between building and losing confidence makes cycles of failure easier to enter and cycles of success harder to establish and sustain. The resources and opportunities that success brings can widen this gap further.

We often attribute persistence to willpower, but everyone has limits. Even someone who has been resilient and successful can be overwhelmed by later setbacks. In my view, placing all hope of overcoming adversity in personal willpower or past success, while overlooking a person’s circumstances and available support, places too much faith in the power of the mind and falls short of an adequate scientific methodology.

A paper that gave me inspiration was by Zhou and colleagues in Science: History of winning remodels thalamo-PFC circuit to reinforce social dominance (2017). Under experimental conditions, repeated wins strengthened connections in a particular brain circuit in mice, helping them maintain an advantage in later contests. Put simply, winning left a trace in the brain that affected how they competed next.

Another finding in the paper stayed with me: artificially activating the relevant brain region made previously subordinate mice compete more actively and even defeat opponents that had previously beaten them. In this experiment, their past record did not fully determine their later performance. I want to keep asking: could we find an approach that helps people take the actions a successful person would take, even after failure?

A purely imagined victory cannot solve this problem either. In Lu Xun’s The True Story of Ah Q, Ah Q can recast defeat as victory in his mind and find temporary comfort, while his actual circumstances remain unchanged. If that explanation encourages avoidance or disregard for feedback, change may become harder. Comfort can offer a moment to recover; it cannot replace the judgment and action needed to address a problem.

I want to spend my life looking for a more fundamental approach: one that helps people with different personalities and histories of success and failure sustain the ability to face reality, take the actions a successful person would take, and gradually improve their lives, with as little dependence as possible on exceptional willpower or endurance.

AI is changing work and may unsettle the ways many people earn a living, gain recognition, and understand who they are. When skills built over many years are no longer needed, how can a person understand their own value and find a direction in which to act? The urgency of this question extends far beyond my own life. It concerns growing numbers of people, and how humanity will live through these changes.

For me, this is also part of what pursuing a Doctor of Philosophy means: taking an important question seriously without restricting the search for answers to a single discipline. I hope to bring a different perspective through what I have learned about artificial intelligence, memory, and learning.
